content: The indoor-mapping-wayfinding architecture standards enumerate the graph-digitisation failure modes precisely. (1) The centroid graph trap: one node per room, one edge per shared opening - topologically correct, shortest-path works immediately, but the rendered polyline runs straight through walls and the route 'reads to a user as a broken product'; centroid-to-centroid distance also understates the real walk badly in L-shaped corridors. Fix: door nodes at the centre of each opening plus a short perpendicular 'spur' (~0.6m) to the corridor skeleton, charged as real distance. (2) Junction nodes must come from the skeleton, not the rooms - 'a graph without junction nodes can route perfectly and cannot give directions', because there is nothing to hang a 'turn left' on. (3) Vertical nodes (stairs, lifts, escalators) exist on every level the transition serves and are joined by edges that no single level's geometry describes; served levels must come from the transition record, never from geometry, or a lift gets edges to floors it does not stop at. (4) Escalators are the one case where a purely undirected model breaks - model as a directed edge. (5) Verification is a gate, not an afterthought: exactly one connected component across the whole building's level set, zero orphan nodes, per-profile reachability. 'A graph that fails any of these is not published, because a disconnected graph produces the single most damaging user-visible failure: a route that cannot be found between two places a person can clearly walk between.' A disconnected graph is a failure, not a warning - anything that logs and continues will eventually publish a building with a stranded wing. (6) The commonest concrete cause of a 2-component graph is an opening whose space reference does not resolve, so a room was never joined to the corridor. (7) Double doors modelled as two openings produce two parallel edges and odd instructions - merge openings closer than ~0.4m into one node. (8) Corridors longer than ~15m need an intermediate node. (9) Rooms with no opening create orphan space nodes - fail the level. (10) Route length systematically under-reports because the centreline cuts corners - at 1m densification, under-reporting is 1.4m per corner. The NavVis Navigation Graph Quality Checklist adds operational checks: fully connected, no disconnected clusters, floors connected via the corresponding stairs, corridors modelled as straight lines of nodes, stair nodes above floor nodes, no nodes placed on tables, minimal node count with consistent spacing and no two nodes too close. The ISPRS 2016 floor-plan extraction paper confirms the same class of issues in real digitised CAD data (gaps between lines, false break/overlap points, hanging edges, loss of semantic information) and concludes that exception handling and tuning are always mandatory because production data is never flawless.
